# **30 YEARS OF TRUST AND EXCELLENCE** 

In 1995, a thought took root—quiet, deliberate— Probity Research and Services Private Limited, born not in haste, but in honesty, in the discipline of asking the right questions. 

From those measured beginnings, we did not rush— _we unfolded_ . Insight turned to action, purpose found its scale, and in time, we came to be known as IIFL Finance Limited— a name carried forward on the strength of trust, on the steadiness of prudence, on the quiet confidence of doing things right. 

Thirty years have passed, and we have continuously reinvented ourselves. We have listened to the pulse of a changing India, and learned to move with it— shaping ourselves, reshaping our path. From research to reach, from ideas to impact— gold loans that unlock value, home loans that help provide shelter, MSME finance that fuels enterprises, microfinance that carries hope to the edges of possibility. 

Ours has never been a journey of chance. 

It has been chosen— 

a thoughtful turn towards secured lending, 

a portfolio crafted with care, 

a framework of governance 

that stands firm, even when cycles shift. 

Through seasons of uncertainty, we have held our ground— guarding quality, embracing technology, extending our reach without losing our essence. 



“30 Years of Trust and Excellence”— not just a line, but a lived truth. Trust, earned quietly, one relationship at a time. Excellence, pursued patiently, through rigour, through resolve.

In business, this reflects the power of staying true to one’s core purpose and values—sustainable success comes from authenticity, not imitation. And now, at the threshold of a new decade, we step forward— clear in vision, steady in purpose— rooted in secured lending, strengthened by governance, carried ahead by the force of technology. 

This is not merely time gone by. 

## It is resilience, it is reinvention, it is responsibility, 

etched into every step that we have taken. 

A foundation laid with care— not just to endure, but to rise, to lead, and to become what tomorrow demands.

#### **OUR ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE** 

## **THREE DECADES OF TRUST, ANCHORED BY ORGANIZATIONAL EXCELLENCE** 

Our material subsidiaries, IIFL Home Finance and IIFL Samasta Finance Limited, are central to expanding our retail lending franchise. With focused strengths in home loans and microfinance, they enhance our reach across diverse and underserved segments, strengthening our geographic presence and reinforcing a well-diversified, customer-centric lending platform. 

### **IIFL HOME FINANCE LIMITED** 

### **IIFL SAMASTA FINANCE LIMITED** 

IIFL Home Finance Limited is one of India’s leading technology-driven, retail-focused housing finance companies, dedicated to supporting first-time homebuyers from the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS), Medium Income Groups (MIG) and  Low-Income Groups (LIG). The company operates through an extensive network of 315 branches across 18 states and 2 Union Territories. With a strong focus on underserved and and predominantly affordable housing markets in Tier 2 cities and beyond, IIFL Home Finance is committed to expanding access to homeownership for aspiring families across India. 

IIFL Samasta Finance Limited, a prominent NBFCMFI, delivers microfinance solutions across rural and semi-urban regions. With a strong focus on financial inclusion and grassroots entrepreneurship, it empowers underserved communities and supports sustainable socio-economic development. With a network of over 1,614 branches, the company continues to expand its reach and deepen its impact across diverse geographies.

### **OUR COMPETITIVE MOAT** 

#### **Strong Balance Sheet, financials** 

#### **Deep management expertise** 

We are backed by a seasoned leadership team and distinguished Board members from institutions such as RBI, NABARD, HDFC and ICICI Bank, bringing deep expertise across lending, governance, technology and risk management. This strong leadership foundation has enabled us to scale our retail-focused franchise to an AUM of ₹1.08 lakh crore with sustained operational discipline. 

Our strong financial position is supported by a healthy consolidated capital adequacy ratio of 25.3%, provision coverage of 93% and a liquidity buffer of ₹6,638 Crores as of March 31, 2026. With controlled net gearing of 3.8x and a diversified funding mix across banks, debentures, securitisation and co-lending partnerships, we remain well-positioned to drive scalable and capitalefficient growth. 

#### **Rigorous risk, compliance and control** 

#### **Trusted brand and market leader** 

We follow a disciplined approach to risk management through strong underwriting standards, proactive compliance practices and robust internal controls. Supported by AI-led fraud detection and continuous portfolio monitoring, we maintained healthy asset quality with GNPA at 1.5%, NNPA at 0.7% and provision coverage at 93% as of March 31, 2026. 

Over the years, we have strengthened our position as a trusted, customer-centric and technology-enabled NBFC through a strong mix of ATL, BTL and digital initiatives. Backed by a network of 4,829 branches serving over 4.6 Million customers across India, along with vernacular outreach and hyperlocal engagement in Tier II and III markets, we continue to deepen customer trust, expand market presence and enhance brand visibility across underserved segments. 

#### **Operational and technological excellence** 

IIFL Finance continues to strengthen operational efficiency through a robust phygital model and AI-led transformation across underwriting, collections, customer engagement and fraud detection. Our AI-driven lead engine generates a monthly pipeline of nearly ₹1,000 Crores, while multilingual digital interfaces across 22 languages and AI-powered branch productivity tools are enhancing customer experience, scalability and operational agility.

# Dear Stakeholders, 

reaffirming India’s position as one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies. Consumption demand stayed firm, credit offtake from retail and MSME segments — structurally underpenetrated and rich with opportunity — continued to expand at a healthy pace. Encouragingly, asset quality trends showed meaningful improvement, with the industry wide GNPA ratio declining to ~2.9%, reflecting stronger portfolio discipline and better borrower performance across the system. Also, elevated gold prices further provided a favourable backdrop for the gold loan industry, enhancing collateral values, supporting higher loan disbursements, and driving steady growth in assets under management. 

#### **MACRO-ECONOMIC OVERVIEW** 

The global economy faced a turbulent year — geopolitical tensions deepened, trade flows fragmented, and central banks navigated the difficult balance between growth and inflation. The escalating US-Iran conflict sent energy prices sharply higher, straining shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz and sending shockwaves across commodity, currency, and credit markets. 

It is my privilege to present to you the Integrated Annual Report for FY 2025-26, a year that marks 30 Years of Trust and Excellence of our institution. Three decades in financial services is a significant milestone, where cycles are unforgiving and reputations are hard earned. 

As I reflect on our journey from a small, ambitious team in 1995 to a leading retail-focused NBFC serving over 4.6 Million customers across 4,829 branches, what stands out most is not just the scale we built, but the character we have built alongside it. Trust is not a marketing claim. It is the slow accumulation of small decisions made correctly, year after year, especially in the difficult ones. FY 2025-26 was a defining one for our institution, and I believe we honoured the trust placed in us at every step. 

India was not insulated from these pressures. Wholesale inflation rose to 8.3% in April, the rupee faced periodic headwinds, and short-term funding markets felt the stress of imported inflation. 

### **_<u>Yet, India’s story remained one of extraordinary resilience.</u>_** 

**PORTFOLIO RESET AND ASSET QUALITY IMPROVEMENT** 

GDP growth held strong at 7.4%, 

Last year, in the wake of the regulatory 

intervention on our gold loan business, we made a clear commitment to you: we would emerge from this period not just compliant, but structurally stronger. I am proud to report that this commitment has been delivered in full. 

We made hard choices through the year. We scaled down higher-risk unsecured exposures. We exited businesses where the risk-return profile no longer met our standards. We strengthened our provisioning architecture, moved decisively to an ECL-aligned framework, and invested heavily in early-warning systems and AI-led fraud detection. 

Our microfinance subsidiary, IIFL Samasta, weathered sector-wide stress without retreating from its mission. We worked alongside vulnerable borrowers, supported them through a difficult cycle, and resumed disbursements with enhanced safeguards. The portfolio today is stable, asset quality is improving, and growth is being calibrated carefully. 

#### **GOLD LOAN LEADERSHIP, SECURED RETAIL FOCUS** 

If one chapter of this year’s story stands above the rest, it is the remarkable journey of our gold loan business. From the regulatory pause of March 2024, to a period of introspection and rebuilding, to emerging in FY 2025-26 as the single largest growth engine of the consolidated franchise — this arc captures everything we believe about how institutions should respond to setbacks. 

The story is not just about volume. It is about how the volume was built. We rebuilt systems, retrained branches, recalibrated underwriting, and embedded AI-powered ornament authentication and fraud detection across our network. 

#### **GOVERNANCE, COMPLIANCE AND RISK DISCIPLINE** 

Strengthening governance, compliance, and risk discipline remained a key priority during the year. We enhanced policy frameworks, compliance monitoring, and risk management practices aligned with evolving regulatory expectations. Supported by technology-enabled oversight and strong Board governance, our disciplined approach strengthened organizational resilience, safeguarded stakeholder interests, and reinforced our commitment to sustainable growth. 

#### **STRATEGIC OUTLOOK** 

As we step into FY 2026-27, our strategic framework is simple, and we call it resilient, capital-efficient growth. Our AI transformation is already producing tangible results and that will compound in value over the years ahead. 

We will also continue to scale our colending franchise meaningfully. The new RBI Co-Lending Directions, 2025 have brought welcome clarity to the framework, and we are well positioned to take advantage of the expanded scope across both PSL and non-PSL categories. 

#### **VOTE OF THANKS** 

This year also marks the retirement of our Chairperson, Mr. A. K. Purwar, after more than seventeen years of distinguished service to this institution. His wisdom, integrity, and steady leadership have shaped the character of this Company and guided us through some of our most challenging moments. While he steps away from formal responsibilities, he 

remains a mentor and inspiration to us all. On behalf of the entire IIFL family, I extend our heartfelt gratitude and deepest respect. 

**To our customers** , your trust has been the foundation on which everything else stands. We do not take it for granted. 

**To our regulators** , your scrutiny has made us a stronger, more responsible institution. We are grateful for the rigor you bring. 

**To our investors and shareholders** your conviction during a year of challenge reflects a long-term belief in this enterprise that we are determined to honor. 

**To our partners** the banks who colend with us, the technology providers who power our platforms, the auditors and advisors — thank you for walking alongside us. 

**And, to the members of the IIFL family** , you are the foundation of our success. Your commitment, professionalism, and customer-first mind-set have shaped our journey over the past three decades and strengthened the trust we enjoy today. 

We emerge from FY 2025-26 stronger, sharper, and more aligned than ever with the mission that started this journey thirty years ago — to democratize access to finance and build a more inclusive economy. The road ahead is long, but the foundation is firm. The storms will come, as they always do. We will be ready. 

Warm Regards,

## **FY26: PERFORMANCE IN NUMBERS** 

FY 2025-26 delivered a meaningful recovery across all key parameters. Consolidated Loan AUM reached ₹1,08,180 Crores, growing 38% yearon-year and crossing the ₹1 Lakh Crore mark for the first time. Full-year Profit After Tax stood at ₹1,817 Crores, up 214% year-on-year. Q4 Profit After Tax (PAT, pre-NCI) reached ₹623 Crores, up 148% year-on-year, with 

Three decades in financial services is a significant reckoning. Markets rise and fall. Regulations evolve. Technology disrupts business models that once seemed permanent. Through every such shift, the discipline that has sustained this institution has remained constant — a commitment to trust 

pre-provision operating profit growing 80% year-on-year in the quarter. Gold loan AUM reached ₹52,581 Crores, up 150% year-on-year — albeit on a lower base in FY25 that was affected by the regulatory embargo — with IIFL Finance re-established as one of India’s leading gold loan NBFCs. Asset quality improved materially: Gross NPA at 1.5%, Net NPA at 0.7%, and provision coverage ratio at 93%. 

These numbers follow the most challenging period in the Company’s history. That they have been delivered with improved asset quality and a strengthened balance sheet reflects the institutional resilience built over three decades. The successful issuance of a USD 500 Million Social Bond — the largest in IIFL Finance’s history — with strong international institutional demand, reflects the confidence that global capital markets continue to place in this franchise. 

## **TECHNOLOGY AND AI: PUTTING CAPABILITY TO WORK** 

Technology has been integral to IIFL Finance’s operating model for several years. In FY 2025-26, artificial intelligence moved from planning into active deployment — in lead generation, in gold ornament authentication, in credit underwriting, and in collections and customer service. Each of these applications is improving speed, accuracy, and risk outcomes in ways that benefit both customers and the business. Investment in technology will continue to deepen, with AI embedded more widely across the credit lifecycle in the years ahead. 

The direction is clear: lending institutions that use data and AI to serve customers with greater precision and lower cost will be better positioned for the 

decade ahead. IIFL Finance has made meaningful progress on this path. 

**SERVING THE BHARAT THAT FORMAL FINANCE HAS BARELY REACHED** 

Hundreds of millions of creditworthy Indians — the self-employed artisan, the small trader, the first-time homebuyer in a growing town — remain outside the reach of formal finance. Not for want of creditworthiness, but for want of institutions willing and able to serve them with appropriate products, fair pricing, and genuine last-mile presence. 

IIFL Finance’s gold loan franchise serves predominantly the self-employed Indian who holds gold but carries little formal credit history, with branches in markets that formal banking has not fully reached. The home loan subsidiary supported over 5,200 beneficiaries under the PMAY 2.0 affordable housing scheme in FY 2025-26, extending access to buyers in tier-2 and tier3 India. Both businesses have clear structural headroom ahead. Driving financial inclusion for the underbanked and unbanked, from economically weaker sections and geographically underdeveloped areas of our country, is not incidental to this business. It is the business. 

## **CULTURE, EXCELLENCE, AND THE OWNER MINDSET** 

Behind every metric in this report is a culture and set of values consistently adhered to over thirty years — not assembled overnight. IIFL Finance’s values of Fairness, Integrity, and Transparency are not aspirational statements. They are operating disciplines, embedded in how credit decisions are made, how customers are served, and how every commitment to every stakeholder is honored. The owner mindset that runs through this 

organization — where every colleague treats the customer’s trust and the Company’s capital with the same care they would their own — reflects thirty years of deliberate investment in people and values. 

Excellence, in this context, means holding the same standard in governance, underwriting, and customer engagement every single day, regardless of conditions. It is this culture, as much as any product or platform, that has kept this institution grounded through difficulty and capable of delivery when conditions improve. 

FY 2025-26 also marked the retirement of Mr. A. K. Purwar as Chairperson, after more than seventeen years of distinguished service to this institution. His counsel, integrity, and steady leadership guided IIFL Finance through some of its most defining moments. On behalf of the entire IIFL family, we extend our deepest gratitude and respect. 

We are privileged to welcome Mr. B. P. Kanungo as the incoming Chairperson. Mr. Kanungo brings exceptional institutional experience, including a distinguished tenure as Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India. His regulatory depth and understanding of financial systems will be of considerable value as IIFL Finance continues to strengthen its governance and compliance culture. 

To our customers, investors, lenders, banking partners, regulators, and every member of the IIFL team: thirty years of this institution’s strength is a reflection of your trust. We remain committed to honoring it.

# **GOLD LOANS: THE CORE REBOUND ENGINE** 

# **REBUILDING STRENGTH. RESTORING MOMENTUM.** 

The RBI’s restrictions on IIFL Finance’s gold loan disbursements in FY 2023-24, arising from process-level observations in the gold loan business, marked a significant inflection point for us. The embargo continued to impact business momentum during FY 2024-25, particularly across the gold loan franchise, which historically remained a key contributor to the retail lending portfolio. 

Following the lifting of the embargo effective September 19, 2024, we undertook a calibrated recovery strategy centered on governance strengthening, secured lending expansion, tighter risk management and capital-efficient growth. FY 2025-26 consequently emerged as a year of operational recovery, robust profitability improvement and portfolio realignment, supported by disciplined execution across businesses.

#### **UNLOCKING EMERGING OPPORTUNITIES** 

# **THREE DECADES OF FINANCIAL INCLUSION AND PROGRESS** 

### **GOLD LOAN MARKET EXPANSION** 

#### **Rapid portfolio Rising ticket sizes and expansion borrower participation** 

India’s gold loan industry has witnessed accelerated growth over the last few years, with the overall portfolio expanding by nearly 3.8x since March 2022. Gold loans now account for 11.1% of the retail credit portfolio, making it the second-largest retail lending segment after housing loans. Additionally, rising gold prices significantly increased gold collateral values, leading to higher gold loan ticket sizes and overall portfolio expansion. 

The segment has seen a sharp increase in origination activity, with origination volumes growing by 2.3x and origination value increasing by 5.1x between 2022 and 2025. Average ticket sizes have more than doubled from approximately ₹ 90,000 to ₹ 1.96 lakh, supported by higher collateral valuations and growing borrower confidence. Moreover, the organized gold loan market demonstrated substantial growth, reaching a valuation of ₹ 7.1 Lakhs Crores in FY 2023-24 and is expected to reach around ₹ 14.19 Lakhs Crores by FY 2028-29 at a CAGR of 14.85%.

### **UNDERPENETRATED AFFORDABLE HOUSING FINANCE** 

India’s affordable housing finance market continues to offer strong long-term growth potential, supported by low mortgage penetration, rising housing demand and Government initiatives such as ‘Housing for All’. According to ICRA, the AUM of Affordable Housing Finance Companies (AHFCs) increased by 19% YoY to ₹1.58 Lakhs Crores in 9M FY 2025-26, driven by healthy demand across affordable housing and LAP segments. 

**19% YoY AUM growth During 9M FY 2025-26** 

## **19–21%** 

**Expected industry growth in FY 2026 and FY 2027** 

The sector remains significantly underpenetrated across underserved and semi-urban markets, creating substantial headroom for growth. ICRA expects the AHFC industry to maintain a healthy 19–21% growth trajectory in FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27, supported by improving income levels, increasing formalization of credit, and sustained housing demand. 

**₹1.58 lakh crore AHFC industry AUM** 



### **STRUCTURAL GROWTH IN RETAIL CREDIT** 

NBFCs in India continued to play a pivotal role in driving retail credit expansion in FY 2025-26, complementing the banking system amid moderated but steady overall credit growth. Retail lending remained a core focus area for NBFCs, supported by rising consumption demand, formalization trends (e.g., gold loans), and NBFCs' agility in serving underserved segments like MSMEs, vehicle finance, and smaller-ticket retail borrowers. 

Retail assets constituted around 56-58% of NBFC lending (up significantly from earlier years), estimated at over ₹16 lakh crore with double-digit CAGR. NBFC-Retail AUM (excluding Housing Finance Companies) grew at a moderated but healthy pace— around 17-19% in H1 FY 2025-26, with full-year expectations in the 16-18%. ICRA projected retail AUM crossing ₹30 lakh crore by FY 2026-27.

### **MSME FORMALIZATION & CREDIT GAP** 

The increasing formalisation of MSMEs is expanding the addressable credit market for lenders. Rising GST registrations, digital payment adoption, UPI penetration, and broader use of formal banking channels are improving financial transparency and enabling better borrower assessment. As per Government estimates, GST registrations have crossed 1.5 crore, reflecting the growing integration of small businesses into the formal economy. 

# **1.5 Crore** 

##### **MSME registered under GST** 

Despite this progress, the MSME sector continues to face a substantial credit gap. India’s MSME financing gap exceeds US$ 530 Billion, with a significant share of small enterprises still dependent on informal borrowing channels due to limited collateral, insufficient credit history and restricted access to organized finance.

## **KEEPING BUSINESS MOMENTUM ALIVE**

_Recognizing the importance of maintaining liquidity, he turned to IIFL Finance Gold Loans to bridge temporary cash flow gaps and ensure uninterrupted business operations. The facility provided quick access to funds whenever inventory replenishment was required, helping him meet customer demand without compromising on service levels._ 

_The convenience of digital top-up facilities further strengthened his ability to respond to business opportunities in real time. By enabling easy access to liquidity against existing gold collateral, IIFL Finance continues to support entrepreneurs like Gaurav in maintaining operational continuity and pursuing business growth with confidence._

#### **Customer Income Profile** 

Focused on advancing financial inclusion, 87% of customers belong to income groups earning below ₹3 lakh annually, reflecting a strong presence across economically weaker sections (EWS) and underserved communities. 

#### **Branch Distribution Profile** 

Our branch network continues to maintain a strong presence beyond metropolitan markets, with 84% of branches located across semi-urban, urban and rural regions, enabling deeper penetration into underserved and high-growth Bharat markets. 

This diversified business framework constitutes a structural competitive moat for IIFL Finance Limited, enabling superior risk dispersion and portfolio resilience. By mitigating concentration risks and reducing cyclicality across business segments, the model ensures continuity of growth momentum, even amid volatility in individual verticals, thereby reinforcing earnings stability and longterm value creation.

IIFL Finance Limited has built a differentiated phygital distribution model that seamlessly integrates an expansive physical footprint with advanced digital capabilities. As of March **4,829** 31, 2026, we operate a network of ~4,800+ branches, serving over 4.6 Million customers, **Branches** enabling deep and granular penetration across urban, semi-urban and rural markets. 

This on-ground reach is augmented by AI-led underwriting, proprietary digital platforms and paperless processes, driving faster turnaround times, enhanced customer **4.6 Million+** experience and efficient risk assessment. **Customers** 

During the year, we undertook decisive actions to enhance portfolio resilience, including exit from higher-risk segments such as digital unsecured MSME, Micro LAP and select microfinance geographies, alongside a one-time portfolio clean-up in housing finance. This has resulted in a more resilient portfolio, lower volatility and improved risk-adjusted returns. 

Our risk framework is further fortified through AI-led early warning systems, continuous portfolio surveillance and disciplined collection mechanisms, enabling timely identification and mitigation of emerging risks. Additionally, Stage 2 and Stage 3 assets continue to trend downward, indicating sustained improvement in underlying asset quality. 

This sharp focus on risk selection, secured lending and governance discipline has enabled us to progressively lower credit costs, with a clear trajectory towards sub-2% levels, while strengthening portfolio stability and long-term earnings visibility. 

IIFL Finance is also strengthening risk governance through advanced technology, AI-powered image fraud detection systems are being leveraged to assess and flag suspicious gold ornament images for field audits. The initiative enhances fraud monitoring capabilities, enables faster risk identification and reinforces control mechanisms across gold loan operations.

# **A SECOND CHANCE THAT SPARKED SUCCESS** 

_Randheer Singh Gorarandhawa from Amritsar began his entrepreneurial journey with a simple vision of building a milk distribution business. The initial days were filled with uncertainty, and his first attempt yielded disappointing results. Having already pledged his family’s gold to raise capital, the setbacks could easily have ended his entrepreneurial ambitions._ 

_Instead, timely support from IIFL Finance helped him stay committed to his goal. By extending additional funding against the same collateral at lower interest rate and encouraging him to persevere, IIFL Finance provided both financial assistance and confidence at a critical stage of his journey._ 

_With renewed determination, he gradually expanded his operations and successfully established multiple milk retail outlets. His story is a testament to resilience, hard work, and the importance of having a dependable financial partner. Today, his thriving business stands as proof that access to timely credit can help transform challenges into opportunities and aspirations into lasting success._

# **OVER THREE DECADES** 

Risk management forms an integral part of IIFL Finance’s organizational framework. We follow a comprehensive and proactive approach towards identifying, assessing and mitigating risks across all areas of our business operations. Our approach is centered on strengthening resilience through robust risk mitigation practices, strict regulatory compliance and the promotion of a strong culture of accountability, governance and risk awareness across the organization. 

## **INTEGRATED RISK GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK** 

Our Company has a globally recognized ‘Three Lines of Defense’ model, the framework ensures clear accountability, independent oversight and effective control mechanisms across all business operations, enabling proactive risk identification, mitigation and regulatory compliance.

## **DEFINED BENEFIT OBLIGATIONS AND EMPLOYEE RETIREMENT PLANS** 

- Employee benefit obligations are administered through both defined contribution and defined benefit retirement schemes, including Provident Fund and Gratuity Plans. Contributions towards Provident Fund are recognized on an accrual basis, while gratuity liabilities are fully funded through an independent trust structure. The Company undertakes periodic actuarial evaluations using the Projected Unit Credit Method to ensure appropriate provisioning and effective oversight of postretirement benefit obligations. 

## **GOVERNMENT-SUPPORTED FINANCIAL INCLUSION INITIATIVES** 

- Although no direct financial support has been received from the Government, various institutional schemes and guarantee programs such as NAPS, CGTMSE and CGFMU continue to create an enabling ecosystem for business growth. These frameworks help strengthen credit outreach, enhance access to finance for underserved segments and support the broader objective of inclusive economic development. 

## **~~CLIMATE-RELATED RISKS, OPPORTUNITIES AND FINANCIAL~~ IMPLICATIONS** 

- Evolving climate-related regulations and rising sustainability expectations are reshaping the operating environment for financial institutions, creating both challenges and emerging growth avenues. While increased compliance requirements may influence operational costs, the transition towards sustainable and inclusive finance is opening new opportunities across affordable housing and financial inclusion. Through IIFL Home Finance and IIFL Samasta, we continue to advance responsible lending practices aligned with long-term sustainable development goals. 

## **NAVIGATING CHALLENGES WITH RESILIENCE** 

- Amid a dynamic operating landscape in FY 2025-26, the Company navigated macroeconomic pressures and regulatory challenges, including temporary restrictions on gold loan disbursements by the Reserve Bank of India. Through focused execution, effective liquidity management and a successfully subscribed rights issue, we further strengthened our financial resilience and enhanced our readiness to capitalize on future growth opportunities.

## **PRODUCT & PROCESS TRAINING**

# **SAMPAT DEVI’S JOURNEY TOWARDS FINANCIAL INDEPENDENCE** 

_Driven by a desire to improve her family’s financial wellbeing, Sampat Devi from Nagaur, Rajasthan, aspired to establish a small retail venture that could provide a steady and sustainable source of income. However, limited financial resources made it challenging to turn her dream into reality._ 

_With the support of IIFL Samasta Finance Limited, she was able to open a grocery store and gradually grow the business through consistent effort, prudent financial management and timely loan repayments. Over time, she earned the trust of customers and strengthened her presence within the community._ 

_Today, the grocery store stands as a reliable source of livelihood, contributing significantly to her family’s financial security and resilience. Her journey demonstrates how access to timely financial support can empower women entrepreneurs to build sustainable livelihoods and create lasting economic impact for their households._

# **AI-LED UNDERWRITING AND CREDIT SYSTEMS** 

Artificial intelligence is increasingly at the core of how we evaluate credit, manage risk and serve customers. Our AI and machine learning models are deployed across the lending lifecycle — from initial credit assessment and underwriting to realtime portfolio monitoring, collections prioritization and cross-sell recommendations. 

## **KEY CAPABILITIES IN DEVELOPMENT AND DEPLOYMENT:** 

   - AI-powered copilots being developed using Copilot Studio for employee-assisted and customer-facing conversational interfaces across lending workflows 

- AI-driven underwriting models that incorporate bureau data, transaction history and behavioral signals for faster, more accurate credit decisions 

   - Machine learning models supporting collections prioritization, reducing cost-to-collect and improving recovery rates 

- Predictive risk models and early warning systems deployed to identify portfolio stress signals before they Model governance, validation and monitoring become delinquencies — supporting our strong GNPA frameworks ensuring accuracy, auditability and biastrajectory free decisioning across all AI systems 

# **CYBERSECURITY AND TECHNOLOGY RESILIENCE** 

Protecting customer data and securing our information systems are foundational to our business continuity and to the trust our customers place in us. Our cybersecurity architecture is designed around a defense-in-depth philosophy — with layered controls, continuous monitoring and board-level governance — ensuring that we are proactive, not reactive, in the face of an evolving threat landscape. 

### **Framework / Control** 

### **Description** 

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 aligned Information Security Management System (ISMS); NIST **Governance & Standards** Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (Govern–Identify–Protect–Detect–Respond–Recover); CIS Critical Security Controls; ISO 22301 Business Continuity Management. "Never trust, always verify" — continuous authentication and authorization of all users, **Zero Trust Architecture** devices and systems. Reinforced through a defense-in-depth strategy with controls across network, application, endpoint and data layers. 

Next-Generation Anti-Virus (NGAV), advanced malware threat detection, Privileged **Advanced Security Controls** Access Management (PAM), Data Loss Prevention (DLP), encryption, virtual patching and OWASP-aligned secure development practices across all applications and APIs. Next-generation Security Operations center (SOC) with AI-driven analytics for real-time **24x7 AI-Driven SOC** threat detection, analysis and response; integrated with threat intelligence from CERT-In, FS-ISAC, and curated threat feeds. Brand Protection Service proactively monitors the external digital ecosystem for **Brand & Digital Protection** phishing, impersonation, look-alike domains, fake applications and fraudulent social media activity, with rapid takedown capabilities. 10+ security audits annually; bi-annual penetration testing by CERT-In empanelled **Testing & Resilience** independent auditors; periodic cyber drills and simulation exercises to validate incident response preparedness; Application Security Lifecycle Management (ASLM) framework. CTO and CISO lead execution of cybersecurity strategy with regular reporting to **Board-Level Oversight** the Board. IT Strategy Committee, IT Steering Committee, and Information Security Committee provide multi-layered governance.

# **CASE STORIES** 

When Ram Rawat (name changed) arrived at Manav Shelter Home in 2022, he faced immense challenges. Having lost his mother and been abandoned by his father, he grew up in a difficult environment with limited support. Despite being enrolled in Grade 5, Ram was unable to read or write and struggled with behavioral and social issues that made it difficult for him to connect with peers. 

Through remedial education, regular counselling, personalized mentoring, and participation in sports and group activities, Ram gradually rebuilt his confidence and skills. Today, he is a capable student who actively participates in school and social 

activities. His transformation was further reflected when he represented his school in Atya Patya at the Raigad district level, securing first place and bringing recognition to his school. Ram’s journey demonstrates how consistent care, guidance, and opportunity can transform a vulnerable child into a confident and motivated young individual. 

## **FROM STRUGGLE TO SUCCESS – RAM’S JOURNEY OF TRANSFORMATION** 

Every morning, Kamla Meena rows across a lake to reach Bindoda Fala, a remote island with no school, anganwadi, or road connectivity. The journey, often made against changing winds and rough waters, is one she has undertaken for years to run the Sakhiyon Ki Baadi center on the island. 

After completing Class XII, Kamla struggled to find employment and support her family. The opening of the center gave her both a livelihood and a purpose. Through songs, games, and simple lessons, she introduced children—many of whom had never attended school—to the world of learning. 

As attendance grew and families witnessed the impact, education became a regular part of life on the island. The income from the center also enabled Kamla to complete her Bachelor’s degree in July 2024, strengthening her role as a provider for her family. 

Today, Kamla is recognized across Bindoda Fala not only as an educator but as a symbol of determination. In a place separated by water and distance, she ensures that education reaches every child—one boat ride at a time.

## **ENERGY MANAGEMENT** 

Conserving energy across our offices and operations sits at the heart of our environmental approach, delivering both environmental benefits and meaningful cost efficiencies. Our energy management strategy is shaped around three levers: reducing consumption through smart infrastructure, transitioning to renewable sources, and deploying technology for real-time monitoring. 

- Implemented energy-efficient LED lighting with smart sensors across offices and branches 

- Installed solar panels at the IIFL Samasta Head Office Guest House, supporting on-site renewable generation 

- ISO 14001:2015 Environmental Management System certified for three large offices in Mumbai, Thane and Bangalore, driving systematic energy and resource governance 

### **KEY INITIATIVES** 

   - 100% paperless gold loan disbursements, eliminating paper-based processes across our flagship lending business 

- Achieved LEED Gold Certification for our Gurugram headquarters, reflecting best-in-class energy and resource efficiency standards 

   - Adopted access-based printing and default double-sided printing across all offices and branches, reducing paper consumption 

- Adopted the Tata Green Tariff at our Hubtown corporate office, Mumbai, enabling the sourcing of renewable electricity directly from the grid 

   - Using bamboo-based (BECO) tissue paper at the Hubtown Mumbai office, replacing single-use bleached tissue products 

- Deployed an IoT-based energy monitoring system for real-time control of air-conditioning across one large office, delivering measurable energy savings 

## **GHG EMISSIONS** 

Our emissions reporting covers Scope 1 (direct combustion), Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and Scope 3 (business travel, purchased goods, capital goods and waste). Emission factors are drawn from the EPA GHG Emission Factor Hub, CEA CDM CO₂ Baseline Database and DEFRA GHG Conversion Factors. Consolidation is based on the operational control approach. We have started to measure financed emissions of some of our product segments. This step will help us further enhance our environment disclosures, arrive at a baseline and set targets in a gradual manner.

## **EXPANDING ACCESS TO AFFORDABLE AND SUSTAINABLE HOUSING** 

Access to affordable housing and environmental responsibility are closely connected. Homes that use energyefficient materials, improved ventilation and sustainable design reduce long-term costs for homeowners while lowering environmental impact. Our sustainability approach focuses on three priorities: expanding access to affordable housing for underserved communities, encouraging green construction practices in housing projects, and improving resource efficiency within our own operations. Through initiatives such as Kutumb and Humara Kutumb, we work with developers, homeowners 

and local construction ecosystems to promote practical and scalable sustainable housing practices. 

### **EXPANDING ACCESS TO GREEN HOUSING** 

Affordable housing developments increasingly incorporate sustainability considerations such as energy-efficient building materials, water conservation systems and improved ventilation. These projects incorporate features such as energy-efficient building envelopes, improved daylight utilisation, water-efficient plumbing systems and green landscaping, helping reduce energy consumption and improve long-term affordability for homeowners.

# **4. DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY AND DIVIDEND** 

During the year under review, the Board declared and paid an interim dividend of ₹4 per equity share (200%) (i.e. 2 times of the Face Value of 2 per equity share) in accordance with the Dividend Distribution Policy of the Company and relevant provisions of the Companies Act & RBI Act. This led to an outgo of ₹170.09 Crore (including tax deducted at source). The Board recommend that the said interim dividend be considered as final. 

As stipulated in Regulation 43A of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“Listing Regulations”), the Board has adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy which is annexed as **“Annexure I”** to this Report and is available on the website of the Company at <u>https://storage.googleapis.com/iifl-fnance-</u> - <u>storage/fles/2026 05/Dividend_Distribution_Policy.pdf</u> 

# **5. TRANSFER TO INVESTOR EDUCATION AND PROTECTION FUND** 

Pursuant to the provisions of Sections 124 and 125 of the Act read with the Investor Education and Protection Fund (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016, dividends which remain unclaimed/unpaid for a period of 7 years are required to be transferred to Investor Education and Protection Fund (“IEPF”). 

Similarly, in the case of Non-Convertible Debentures (“NCDs”), the unclaimed interest and principal amounts are also required to be transferred to the IEPF Authority within thirty (30) days from the expiry of seven (7) years, as per the relevant provisions of the IEPF. 

During the year under review, the Company transferred to IEPF `10,73,225 on April 4, 2025 being the unclaimed dividend amount pertaining to the FY 2017-18 and ₹5,86,680 on March 17, 2026 being the unclaimed dividend amount pertaining to the FY 2018-19 and also transferred ₹1,16,13,278 to IEPF being the unclaimed interest and principal amount pertaining to NCDs. 

In accordance with the aforesaid provisions, the underlying shares in respect of dividends which remain unpaid/unclaimed for a period of seven consecutive years or more shall be transferred to demat account of the IEPF Authority within thirty days from expiry of the said period. Accordingly, various steps are being taken on an ongoing basis to reach out to the Members, through email and other means, whose shares are due to be transferred to the IEPF, in order to create awareness and provide them an opportunity to claim their unclaimed dividends. In view of the aforesaid, the Company had sent individual notices to the concerned Members and had published the notice in the leading newspapers in English and Regional Language having wide circulation to inform the Members about the transfer of equity shares to demat account of IEPF Authority. In accordance with the above provisions, the Company transferred 8,652 equity shares pertaining to the FY 2017-18 and 3,433 equity shares pertaining to the FY 2018-19 to the demat account of the IEPF Authority, in respect of which the dividend has remained unclaimed for seven consecutive years. 

The list of unpaid dividend is available on the Company’s website at <u>https://www.iif.com/fnance/investorinformation. Members are requested to check the said</u>

In compliance with Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”) Circular No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS-RAC1/P/ CIR/2023/176 dated November 8, 2023, relating to unclaimed amounts in respect of listed Non-Convertible Securities, the Company has put in place a procedural framework for handling unclaimed interest and principal amounts lying with it. # **6. KEY INITIATIVES/DEVELOPMENTS** 

## **a. Public Issue of Non-Convertible Debentures** 

During the year under review, your Company had filed a Shelf Prospectus on March 29, 2025, with the Registrar of Companies and SEBI, to raise through Public Issue of Secured, Rated, Listed, Redeemable NCDs an amount aggregating up to ₹2,500 Crore and Tranche I Prospectus on March 29, 2025 to be read with the Corrigendum to the Tranche I Prospectus dated April 02, 2025 to raise through Public Issue of Secured, Rated, Listed, Redeemable NCDs an amount aggregating up to ₹100 Crore with an option to retain oversubscription of ₹400 Crore. The issue was fully subscribed and these were allotted on April 21, 2025, and are listed and traded on the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”) and BSE Limited (“BSE”). 

Your Company had also filed a Shelf Prospectus on February 12, 2026, with the Registrar of Companies and SEBI, to raise through Public Issue of Secured, Rated, Listed, Redeemable NCDs an amount aggregating up to ₹2,000 Crore and Tranche I Prospectus on February 12, 2026 to raise through Public Issue of Secured, Rated, Listed, Redeemable NCDs an amount aggregating up to ₹500 Crore with an option to retain oversubscription of ₹1,500 Crore. The said NCDs were allotted on March 06, 2026, and are listed and traded on NSE and BSE. 

## **b. Issuance of Non-Convertible Debentures on a Private Placement basis including Perpetual Debt Instrument** 

During the year under review, your Company raised an 

aggregate amount of ₹2,415 crore through the private placement of NCDs. 

The aforesaid amount includes Perpetual Debt Instruments (“PDIs”) aggregating to ₹600 crore. During the year, there was no unpaid interest on your Company's PDIs. Detailed disclosures relating to the PDIs are provided in Note No. 21.2 and 48(i) to the standalone financial statements forming part of this Annual Report. 

These NCDs are listed and traded on the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”). 

Additionally, during the year under review, HFC raised ₹200 Crore through Private Placement of Redeemable NCDs, and Samasta raised ₹1,465 Crore through Private Placement of Redeemable NCDs. The said Privately Placed NCDs issued by HFC and by Samasta are listed and traded on NSE. 

## **c. Bank Refinance** 

During the year under review, HFC had availed ₹500 Crore of refinance facility from National Bank For Agriculture And Rural Development (“NABARD”) under its refinance schemes. 

## **d. Funds raised by way of other Borrowings** 

During the year under review, your Company raised ₹7,918 Crore through term loans from various banks. 

HFC raised ₹2,760 Crore through term loans from various banks and financial institutions. HFC has also raised ₹150 Crore by way of issuance of Commercial Paper. Additionally, HFC raised USD 345 Mn through ECBs amounting to ₹3060.68 Crore from various Development Financial Institutions and Banks. 

Samasta raised ₹2,936.24 Crore, ₹2,326.23 Crore, ₹1,526.69 Crore and ₹130 Crore through Term Loans, Direct Assignment, Securitisation and Commercial Paper respectively from various banks and financial institutions. 

## **e. Revision in International credit rating** 

During the year under review, the international credit ratings from S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings have been revised from B+/stable to B+/Positive. 

# **7. UTILIZATION OF FUNDS** 

During the year under review, your Company successfully raised additional capital through issuance of NCDs on a private placement basis. These funds were raised to support the Company’s growth plans, strengthen its balance sheet, and ensure adequate liquidity to meet operational and regulatory requirements.

# **8. CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY INITIATIVES** 

The Corporate Social Responsibility (“CSR”) Committee of the Board has formulated and recommended to the Board a CSR Policy indicating the CSR activities which can be undertaken by the Company. The Board approved the CSR Policy which is available on the website of the Company at <u>https://storage.googleapis.com/iiflfnance-storage/fles/2023-07/CSR%20policy_IIFL%20 Finance.pdf</u> 

IIFL group has set-up India Infoline Foundation (“IIFL Foundation”), a Section 8 Company incorporated under the Act which acts as the principal arm to undertake CSR initiatives on behalf of your Company and its subsidiary. IIFL Foundation through its CSR initiatives addresses 5 thematic areas – Health, Education and Environment, Livelihood & Poverty Alleviation, collectively – HELP. 

As per Rule 4(2) of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014, IIFL Foundation has registered itself with the Central Government by filing the e-Form CSR-1 with the Registrar of Companies. 

IIFL Foundation has identified focus areas for CSR initiatives which includes: 

- Sakhiyon ki Baadi – A program to promote Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Skill (FLN) among females in Rajasthan. Educating girls from the marginalized communities (Scheduled Tribes/ Scheduled Castes) who are out of school or never been to school. The program has an overall reach with 259 learning centres; 

- Supported ‘Hospitality Training Program (Chef Trade)’ for 120 Kashmiri youth in Kupwara, Jammu & Kashmir, aimed at enhancing employability through vocational skills. The program included both theoretical and practical training sessions, along with placement opportunities and market guidance; 

- Supported ‘Homestay Host Training’ for youth in Tezu, Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh, in collaboration with the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and the Ministry of Defence, Government of India. 120 youth from Arunachal Pradesh benefited from this project; 

- Supported 'Manav Shelter Home' in Panvel, Maharashtra which delivers a holistic care program 

for vulnerable and underprivileged children living in urban slum. 28 children directly benefit from the initiative, receiving essential support including food, shelter, clothing, medical care, and overall wellbeing assistance; 

- Supported Banking Financial Services and Insurance (BFSI) Course that prepares students with the skills and knowledge needed to work in the financial sector. 30 Students from marginalizes background directly benefited from this project; 

- Supported an Annual Medical Camp at Barsana, Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, providing free-of-cost eye check-ups, spectacles, cataract surgeries, and dental treatments (including root canal, extractions, and dentures). The initiative conducted 1,480 eye check-ups and 400 dental check-ups, and also provided meals to 1,400 people; 

- Free Mega Medical Camp at Pandharpur, Solapur, Maharashtra. Medical aid and food support provided for pilgrims coming during Ashadi Ekadashi (July 2025). 11,100 people directly received help from this initiative; 

- Provided primary health care services to the devotees attending Ganpati Festival at LalBaug (Mumbai), offering 24×7 Doctors services. Free health check-ups included basic diagnostics and first-aid to 1,000 individuals; 

- Supported the primary section of Mathrubhoomi High School, Kandivali, Mumbai, enabling access to education for children from marginalized communities living in nearby slum settlements. The initiative directly helps 120 primary students, helping them continue their education and successful transition to upper primary grades; 

- Supporting 5 teacher volunteers in 2 Government Secondary Schools in Udaipur, Rajasthan; 

- Donated 16 Slice C T Scan Machine to the Radiodiagnosis department of Maharana Bhupal Hospital, Udaipur, Rajasthan. In the time period of October 2025- March 2026 the machine has benefited 7147 patients; 

- Donated Fully Automatic Bio Chemistry Analyzer, Dental X-ray machin and Laptop to the Community Healthcare Centre, Khamnore, Rajsamand district, Rajasthan. In the time period of April 2025- March 2026 the Bio Chemistry Analyzer benefited 52 & the Dental Xray Machine benefited 35 patients; 

- Donated High Resolution Manometry & PH-

metry Systems Machine to Department of Gastroenterology to Lokmanya Tilak Municipal General Hospital, Sion Mumbai. The donation enabled the hospital to set up a state-of-the-art G I Mobility Lab, which will benefit more than 100 people/month to avail  the service in a reduced cost; 

- Supported livelihood project for the underprivileged, that converted ocean and land plastic waste into ISO Certified helmets, which were donated to police and civilians in Rajsamand & Udaipur in Rajasthan and Mumbai, Maharashtra. 1250 Helmets were donated to Rajasthan Police and 100 to Maharashtra Traffic Police; 

- Supported education (Tuition fees) of 3 students from lower income families in Maharashtra & Rajasthan; 

- Supported the mid- year capacity building camp of SEWA International Fellowship. The Camp played a crucial role in strengthening the leadership and program management capacities of 22 Sewa Fellows; 

- Organized Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) training sessions in Pune, Maharashtra, and Chennai, Tamil Nadu, to equip professionals with essential life-saving skills. The sessions focused on immediate response during cardiac arrest and correct CPR techniques. A total of 121 individuals directly benefited from this initiative; 

- Supported the upgradation of community hall and public space in Rural Police Campus - Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar (Aurangabad), Maharashtra; 

- Support provided to setup Tattva University, a valuebased, multidisciplinary, research-oriented, deemedto-be-university (Distinct Category) in Maharashtra. 4000+ students and 200+ faculty will benefit from the institute;

which is completely cut off from road connectivity. The initiative included provision of furniture, establishment of a computer lab and installation of solar panels. A total of 35 students benefited, as the school serves as the only access point for education in the entire village;

# **11. FINANCIAL LIQUIDITY** 

From a liquidity standpoint, the Company continues to maintain a strong and resilient position. The Company’s principal sources of liquidity include cash and cash equivalents, along with cash flows generated from our lending and investment activities. During the year under review, the Company took proactive steps to ensure that its liquidity position remained robust and aligned with the operational and regulatory expectations applicable to NBFCs. 

The Company successfully raised capital through the issuance of NCDs, thereby strengthening its liquidity profile. These funds enhanced the Company’s financial flexibility, enabling it to respond swiftly to evolving business needs and pursue strategic opportunities as they arise. 

The Consolidated cash and cash equivalent of your Company as on March 31, 2026, stood at ₹3,328.23 Crores as against ₹2,066.63 Crores in the previous year. The Company continues to maintain a prudent balance between liquidity and return on assets, recognizing the importance of ensuring sufficient liquidity to meet all foreseeable financial and business obligations, while also seeking optimal deployment of funds for revenue generation. 

# **12. INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEMS** 

## **Internal audit and its adequacy:** 

The scope and authority of the internal audit function is well defined and to maintain independence and objectivity in its functions, the internal audit function reports directly to the Audit Committee of the Board. At the beginning of each financial year, an annual RiskBased Internal Audit (“RBIA”) plan is rolled out post approval by the Audit Committee of the Board. The audit plan aims to evaluate the efficacy and adequacy of the internal control system(s) and compliance(s) thereof, robustness of internal processes, policies and accounting procedures, compliance with laws and regulations. The internal audit function, consisting of professionally qualified accountants, engineers, fraud risk and information technology specialists,

Based on the reports of the internal audit function, process owners undertake corrective action in their respective areas. Significant audit observations and corrective actions thereon are presented to the Audit Committee of the Board. 

## **Internal Controls over Financial Reporting:** 

Your Board is of the opinion that internal financial controls with reference to the financial statements were tested and reported adequately and operating effectively. The internal financial controls are commensurate with the size, scale and complexity of operations. The controls were tested during the year and no reportable material weaknesses either in their design or operations were observed. Your Company has put in place robust policies and procedures, which inter alia, ensure integrity in conducting its business, safeguarding of its assets, timely preparation of reliable financial information, accuracy and completeness in maintaining accounting records, prevention and detection of frauds and errors.

# **17. ANTI- BRIBERY AND ANTI-CORRUPTION POLICY** 

Your Company has an Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy (“Policy”) on combating bribery and corruption and to conduct Company’s business in an honest and ethical manner. The Company takes a zero-tolerance approach to bribery, corruption and other forms of unlawful payment (including gifts, hospitality, etc.) and are committed to act professionally, fairly and with integrity in all it’s dealings wherever it operates. The Company is also committed towards implementing and enforcing effective systems to counter bribery and corruption. The Policy prohibits offering, promising, giving or authorizing others to give anything in excess of a certain value, either directly or indirectly, to any person or entity, thereby setting out Company’s standards on bribery and other forms of unlawful payments. 

The policy provides information and guiding principles to prevent any activity or conduct relating to bribery, facilitation payments or corruption and to guide employees to act professionally, fairly and with utmost integrity in all their business dealings and relationships, wherever they operate. 

The Policy requires that the Company do not engage in bribery or corruption in any form and explicitly mentions that the Company will not pay or procure payment of a bribe or unlawful fee to encourage the performance of a task or one which is intended or likely to compromise the integrity of another. The Company will not accept any payment, gift or inducement from a third party which is intended to compromise Company’s integrity. 

Ms. Preeti Kanan, Chief Human Resources Officer (“CHRO”), is also designated as the Chief Anti-Corruption Officer. Any individual may report instances of bribery or corruption by writing to <u>anticorruption@iif.com. The</u> Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy is also available on the Company’s website at <u>https://www.iif.com/ fnance/anti-corruption-policy.</u>

# **23. RISK MANAGEMENT** 

Your Company has a well-defined comprehensive Enterprise Risk Management (“ERM”) Framework in place and a robust organizational structure to identify, assess, measure and monitor risks and strengthen controls to mitigate risks. The Company has established procedures to periodically place before the Risk Management Committee and the Board, the risk assessment and minimization procedures being followed by the Company and steps taken by it to mitigate these risks. ERM has been adopted by the Company which uses defined Key Risk Indicators based on quantitative and qualitative factors. A two-dimensional quantitative heat map has been implemented, which enables the Management to have a comprehensive view of various identified risk areas based on their probability and impact. The Company have initiated adequate Risk training and awareness program to ensure preparedness. 

The composition, terms of reference and powers of the Risk Management Committee are in conformity with the requirements of Regulation 21 of the Listing Regulations and Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Governance) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 and the same has been

# **30. PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT**

## Dividend Distribution Policy 

## **Purpose & Scope** 

IIFL Finance Limited (“the Company”) has in place a Board approved Dividend Distribution Policy covering the Company and the Subsidiaries as adopted on March 01, 2011. Further, pursuant to Regulation 43A of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 has mandated that the top 1000 Companies (in terms of market capitalization) need to have a Dividend Distribution Policy in place. 

Accordingly, this policy is to put into place the norms for the determination and declaration of dividend on equity capital by the Company and its subsidiaries. While considering distribution and payment of dividend, the Company will ensure compliance with all the applicable provisions of the law including provisions of the Companies Act, SEBI, RBI, NHB and Income Tax Rules and Regulations etc. related thereto. 

## **A. Factors/ parameters that would be considered while declaring Dividend** 

- I. The financial parameters that shall be considered while declaring dividend: 

   - While considering the total dividend at Holding Company and at each of the Subsidiaries the following will be taken into account: 

      - a. The business plan and actual performance, the capital requirements, free cash flow, debt equity ratio (considering new capital, ESOPs, retained earnings, minimum net worth requirements as per respective regulatory requirements etc.); 

      - b. Adequacy of profits including the accumulated balance in Profit & Loss account; and 

      - c. Taxes on dividend. 

The Board may consider a higher distribution with adequate justification or on special occasions. 

- II. The circumstances under which the shareholders: 

### **i. May expect dividend:** 

- a. Surplus in Profit & loss (P&L) Statement 

- b. Profits in any Financial Year are more than 10% of the equity capital of the Company 

### **ii. May not expect dividend:** 

- a. If there are losses as per P&L Statement (including accumulated balance in P&L account) 

- b. Profit in the any Financial Year is less than 10% of the equity capital. 

- c. If the total income from business/PAT from its ordinary activities in any Financial Year declines by more than 75% from the previous year. 

- d. If the business is seriously affected and visibility is uncertain. 

III. Internal and external factors that shall be considered for declaration of dividend: 

- **i. Internal Factors:** 

   - a. Projected investment in business/new business 

   - b. Projected investments in Subsidiaries/Associates in the year and next year. 

   - c. Net worth/Capital adequacy as required under respective Regulatory requirements. 

### **ii. External Factors:** 

      - a. State of Economy/ Industry/ Business 

      - b. Statutory Taxes/ levies – Changes in income tax rates, DDT etc. 

- IV. Utilisation of Retained Earnings: 

   - The Company would utilise the retained earnings in a manner which is beneficial to the interest of the company and its stakeholders, including, but not limited to: 

   - i. Proposed Capital expenditure 

   - ii. Investments/acquisitions 

149 

IIFL FINANCE LIMITED 

# **ANNEXURE I TO DIRECTORS’ REPORT** 

## Dividend Distribution Policy 

- iii. General corporate purposes including contingencies 

- iv. Capital restructuring 

- V. Parameters that shall be adopted with regard to various classes of shares: In the absence of any other class of shares and/or shares with differential voting rights, the entire distributable profit for the purpose of declaration of dividend is considered for the equity shareholders. 

### **Periodicity of distribution:** 

On a yearly basis, the Holding and Subsidiary Companies may distribute by way of Interim Dividend/s a substantial portion of the total dividend of the Company. The balance portion will be declared by way of final dividend considering the full year’s accounts and will be paid after the approval of shareholders at the Annual General Meeting of the Company. 

### **Disclosures:** 

- a. This policy will be made available on the Company’s website. 

- b. The policy will also be disclosed in the Company’s annual report. 

## **B. In addition to above parameters, the Company will ensure the compliance with reference to criterias prescribed in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025** 

- I. The Board of Directors of the Company shall, while considering the proposals for dividend, take into account each of the following aspects: 

   - a. Supervisory findings of the Reserve Bank on divergence in classification and provisioning for Non-Performing Assets (NPAs). 

   - b. Qualifications in the Auditors’ Report to the financial statements; and 

   - c. Long term growth plans of the NBFC. 

- II. The Company shall declare dividend if it meets the following minimum prudential requirements: 

   - a. The Company shall have met the minimum capital requirements (refer Annexure 1) (including leverage ratio wherever applicable) prescribed under these Directions in each of the last three financial years including the financial year for which the dividend is proposed. 

   - b. The net NPA ratio shall be less than six percent in each of the last three years, including as at the close of the financial year for which dividend is proposed to be declared. 

   - c. The Company shall comply with the provisions of section 45-IC of the RBI Act, 1934. 

   - d. The Company shall be compliant with the prevailing regulations/ guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank. The Reserve Bank shall not have placed any explicit restrictions on declaration of dividend. 

- III. If the Company meets the eligibility criteria specified in paragraph B.2 above can declare dividend up to a dividend payout ratio of 50 percent. There will be no ceiling on dividend payout ratio for eligible NBFCs that do not accept public funds and have no customer interface. 

- IV. If the Company does not meet the applicable capital ratio (including leverage ratio wherever applicable) requirements and/ or the net NPA ratio requirement as above, for each of the last three financial years, shall be eligible to declare dividend, subject to a cap of 10 percent on the dividend payout ratio, provided the NBFC complies with both the following conditions: 

   - a. meets the applicable minimum capital requirement (including leverage ratio wherever applicable), as per Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 as amended from time to time. in the financial year for which it proposes to pay dividend, and 

   - b. has net NPA of less than four percent as at the close of the said financial year. 

- V. The Board shall ensure that the total dividend proposed for the financial year does not exceed the ceilings specified in these guidelines. The Reserve Bank shall not entertain any request for ad-hoc dispensation on declaration of dividend. 

- VI. The Company shall report details of dividend declared during the financial year as per the format prescribed in Annexure 2. The report shall be furnished within a fortnight after declaration of dividend to the Regional Office of the Department of Supervision of the Reserve Bank.

# **THE ANNUAL REPORT ON CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY (CSR) ACTIVITIES FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR ENDED MARCH 31, 2026** 

[Pursuant to Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 8 of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014] 

# **1. BRIEF OUTLINE ON CSR POLICY OF THE COMPANY:** 

IIFL Finance Limited (the “Company”) ensures that its activities extend beyond business and include initiatives and endeavours for the benefit and development of the community and society. The Company strongly believes that Corporate Social Responsibility (“CSR”) initiatives help to promote inclusive growth and equitable development. 

The CSR Policy and activities of the Company are steered by the same values that guide the business of the Company. It can be summarized in one acronym – FIT, which stands for: 

- **Fairness** in all our transactions 

**Integrity** and Honesty in letter, in spirit and in all our dealings with people 

**Transparency** in all our dealings 

By applying these values to the CSR activities, the Company undertakes initiatives that create sustainable growth and empower underprivileged sections of the society. 

The focus areas prioritized by the Company in its CSR strategy are guided by the philosophy of **HELP** (Health, Education & Environment, Livelihood and Poverty Alleviation). The CSR activities of the Company are executed by India Infoline Foundation (generally referred as “IIFL Foundation”), the Implementing Agency. In line with its philosophy, the Company had undertaken the following activities during FY 2025-26: 

- Sakhiyon ki Baadi – A program to promote Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Skill (FLN) among females in Rajasthan. Educating girls from the marginalized communities (Scheduled Tribes/Scheduled Castes) who are out of school or never been to school. The program has an overall reach with 259 learning centres; 

- Supported  ‘Hospitality Training Program (Chef Trade)’ for 120 Kashmiri youth in Kupwara, Jammu & Kashmir, aimed at enhancing employability through vocational skills. The program included both theoretical and practical training sessions, along with placement opportunities and market guidance; 

- Supported ‘Homestay Host Training’ for youth in Tezu, Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh, in collaboration with the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and the Ministry of Defence, Government of India. 120 youth from Arunachal Pradesh benefited from this project; 

- Supported 'Manav Shelter Home' in Panvel, Maharashtra which delivers a holistic care program for vulnerable and underprivileged children living in urban slum. 28 children directly benefit from the initiative, receiving essential support including food, shelter, clothing, medical care, and overall well-being assistance; 

- Supported Banking Financial Services and Insurance (BFSI) Course that prepares students with the skills and knowledge needed to work in the financial sector. 30 Students from marginalizes background directly benefited from this project; 

- Supported an Annual Medical Camp at Barsana, Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, providing free-of-cost eye check-ups, spectacles, cataract surgeries, and dental treatments (including root canal, extractions, and dentures). The initiative conducted 1,480 eye check-ups and 400 dental check-ups, and also provided meals to 1,400 people; 

- Free Mega Medical Camp at Pandharpur, Solapur, Maharashtra. Medical aid and food support provided for pilgrims coming during Ashadi Ekadashi (July 2025). 11,100 people directly received help from this initiative; 

- Provided primary health care services to the devotees attending Ganpati Festival at LalBaug (Mumbai), offering 24×7 Doctors services. Free health check-ups included basic diagnostics and first-aid to 1,000 individuals; 

- Supported the primary section of Mathrubhoomi High School, Kandivali, Mumbai, enabling access to education for children from marginalized communities living in nearby slum settlements. The initiative directly helps 120 primary students, helping them continue their education and successful transition to upper primary grades; 

- Supporting 5 teacher volunteers in 2 Government Secondary Schools in Udaipur, Rajasthan;

- Provided infrastructure support to Utraj U.P. School in a remote village in Sirohi district, Rajasthan, which is completely cut off from road connectivity. The initiative included provision of furniture, establishment of a computer lab and installation of solar panels. A total of 35 students benefited, as the school serves as the only access point for education in the entire village; 

- Provided support for treatment of a patient from an economically disadvantaged background, Rajsamand, Rajasthan; 

- Supported the establishment of a computer lab at Government Senior Secondary School, Vati, Udaipur, Rajasthan. A total of 257 students benefited, most of whom are from predominantly rural and economically weaker communities; 

- Supported the construction of a conference hall at Army Goodwill School, Trehgam, Kupwara, Jammu & Kashmir for students and staff. A total of 314 students and teachers will benefit, enabling participation in virtual sessions and access to special classes conducted by educationists and experts from across the country; 

- Supported the installation of Solar Panels and a Smart Board at Alakh Ved Gurukul residential school, Chittorgarh, Rajasthan. The initiative helped 100 residential students in the institute; and 

- Gyan Shaala – Education Support Organization provided support to Develop curriculum for Sakhiyon Ki Baadi project which aims to promote Foundational Literacy and numeracy, Udaipur, Rajasthan.

## **INFORMATION RELATING TO CONSERVATION OF ENERGY, TECHNOLOGY ABSORPTION AND INNOVATION AND FOREIGN EXCHANGE EARNINGS/OUTGO FORMING PART OF THE DIRECTORS’ REPORT IN TERMS OF SECTION 134(3)(m) OF THE COMPANIES ACT, 2013.** 

### **Conservation of Energy:** 

- A. Conservation of energy: The Company is engaged in providing financial services and, as such, it’s operations do not account for substantial energy consumption. However, the Company is taking all possible measures to conserve energy. Several environment friendly measures were adopted by the Company. 

   - i. Steps taken / impact on conservation of energy: 

      - Installation of sensor-based lights in common areas. 

      - Installation of capacitors to save power. 

      - Installation of Light Emitting Diode (“LED”) lights for all branches. 

   - ii. Steps taken by the Company for utilising alternate sources of energy: 

      - Use of Green power in corporate office. 

      - Installation of Solar panel in one premise. 

      - Installation of rain harvesting system in 1 premise. 

   - iii. Capital investment on energy conservation equipment: 

      - Installation of access-based network printers to control printing, thereby saving paper. 

      - Installation of IOT based devices to maintain AC temperature across office, thereby saving energy. 

   - iv.  Other measures 

      - Creating environmental awareness by way of distributing the information in electronic/digital form. 

      - Shutting off all lights, when not in use. 

      - Use of bamboo-based housekeeping products. 

The Management frequently puts circulars on the corporate intranet, workplace for its employees, educating them on ways and means to conserve electricity and other natural resources and ensures strict compliance of the same 

### **Technology Absorption and Innovation** 

At IIFL Finance Limited, technology is pivotal to driving our growth, enhancing customer experiences, and strengthening risk management. Leveraging robust digital infrastructure, advanced cybersecurity and innovative solutions such as cloud platforms and AI-driven processes, we remain agile and resilient. Our technological imperatives align strategically, enabling us to deliver secure and seamless financial services in a dynamic digital landscape. 

### **Highlights of the current year (Technology):** 

- Migrated to a unified Flutter-based platform and enhanced cloud infrastructure on Azure with a dedicated subscription for seamless scalability. 

- Implementation of Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA), enhanced 24/7 Security Operations Centre (SOC) and conducted regular cybersecurity drills to strengthen cyber response and resilience. 

- Consolidated chatbot functionalities and streamlined APIs to deliver a consistent and efficient omnichannel experience. 

Piloted Generative AI in service delivery and internal operations to drive efficiency, responsiveness, and future-readiness. 

- Rolled out targeted training programs focused on cybersecurity, emerging technologies and application use to build a digitally capable workforce. 

### **IIFL Loans App:** 

Delivering a seamless and intuitive account management experience. 

Enabling end-to-end digital completion of loan applications. 

- Minimizing documentation through paperless processing.
